replying_to: Replying to RoDesigner: Variation-Aware Optimization for Robust Analog Design with Multi-Task RL
display_title: Official Review of Paper940 by Reviewer cfiF

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a method for automatic analog circuit sizing optimization under process, voltage,
and temperature (PVT) variation. RoDesigner selects the corner tasks and then uses DDPG and PCGrad to tackle multi-task learning for optimizing analog circuits. Full simulation of circuits with PVT is time expensive, the RL algorithm is trained on small sized tasks and it generalizes for full task space. The method is tested against 3 circuits and it demonstrates that it can find solutions with less simulation time, compared to evolutionary search (ES) and Bayesian Optimization (BO). And it can find solutions that are on-par with human designs.
content.main_review:
The paper demonstrates the success of the RL method on analog circuit design under PVT.
AutoCkt also mentions to consider PVT which takes more simulation time. A comparison between RoDesigner and other RL methods applied to analog design would be interesting to see.
It would be also interesting to test on more circuits and analyze if the model can transfer knowledge from one circuit to another. If after training RL on a circuit will later make training on another circuit faster.
One of the main observations is that task space pruning using k-means clustering empirically makes the RL method more sample efficient. Analysis on how much of the task space can be pruned until it doesn't work. Is the pruning of task space different for different circuits?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is concise and clear. It applies RL on analog circuit design and shows that PCGrad and task pruning is beneficial.
Comparison with results from previous work and more analysis on the main method differentials is needed.

replying_to: Replying to RoDesigner: Variation-Aware Optimization for Robust Analog Design with Multi-Task RL
display_title: Official Review of Paper940 by Reviewer GNQf

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes RoDesigner, a multi-task reinforcement learning based circuit design approach. The problem is carefully stated into a machine learning (RL) problem, which considers PVT information and diverse constraints in practice. Task space pruning is adopted to speedup the simulation process. Experiments show that the propsoed method can run efficiently, and the circuit performance can be as good as that of human design, with significanly reduced time cost from several days to hours.
content.main_review:
For me, the paper is mostly about applying multi-task RL to the circuit design problem. The key is to properly adapt the RL training mechanism into the practical problem, by defining the losses and rewards, state and action spaces and practical constraints. While there is not much theoretical guarantees and analysis on the design (e.g., eqn (2) is based on humen expertise), the numerical results suggest that the proposed method could be effective in practical applications.

To be honest, I'm not very familiar with the field of circuit design. Thus, I'm not sure about the common procedures and evaluation for chip design, and how ML/RL has been combined with such problems. It seems that the main novelty as claimed is to consider unpredictable variations in the model by using RL. If this paper is the first one to use RL in circuit design, then I think this could be a good application paper. Otherwise, I don't think the novelty of this paper meets the standard of ICLR.

I would tentatively rate 6. However, I may change the score based on other reviews' commonts on the novelty of the work. Also, though this paper may fit into ML conferences like ICLR, I feel that perhaps it is more suitable to be published at a circuit design related venue.
content.summary_of_the_review: I would tentatively rate 6, but I'm not an expert on circuit design. My score may change based on other experts' comments on the novelty of  the paper.

replying_to: Replying to RoDesigner: Variation-Aware Optimization for Robust Analog Design with Multi-Task RL
display_title: Official Review of Paper940 by Reviewer np4B

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a multitask reinforcement learning method to better design mixed-signal circuits. The method is based on the deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) method, but the main difference lies in the fact that the tasks are pre-classified and task-specific loss functions, instead of single loss function, are used to enlarge learning efficiency as well as efficacy. The feasibility of the proposed method was identified on three benchmark circuits, two-stage OTA, strongARM latch, and folded-cascode OTA. The results ensure the efficiency of the proposed method over the evolutionary strategy (ES), Bayesian optimization (BO), and DDPG methods.
content.main_review:
Strengths: the results are interesting and impressive.

Weaknesses:
Although the present results are interesting and promising, I have the following opinions on the present work.

1. The proposed method appears correct. However, I would like to indicate the unfair comparison with previous works in the manuscript. The key to the improvement in efficiency (in terms of circuit simulation time) is the preprocessing of the data such that the full tasks are classified as small tasks relying on PVT corners. This cost is not considered in the efficiency of the proposed method, so that the efficiency comparison may be unfair in the present manuscript.

2. The novelty of the proposed algorithm is very limited given that the method is merely based on the extension of DDPG to multitasks using multiple loss functions.

3.	I wonder if ICLR is an appropriate conference for the present work. I strongly believe that design-specific conferences, e.g., DAC, are appropriate venues for the present work. The reason is twofold. (1) The proposed method is tailored to a very specific domain (mixed-circuit design). I wonder if the proposed method has scalability to general tasks other than the proposed domain. (2) The proposed method is very technical based on the previous method (DDPG), and thus it is deemed that the contribution of the proposed work to the general RL society is marginal. Regarding the lack of general interest, the impact of the present work is limited.

4.	The key to the improvement in efficiency (in terms of circuit simulation time) is the preprocessing of the data such that the full tasks are classified as small tasks relying on PVT corners. This cost is not considered in the efficiency of the proposed method, so that the efficiency comparison may be unfair in the present manuscript. Additionally, the preprocessing requires quite strong domain knowledge, which may not align with the trend in RL.

5.	The scalability of the proposed method to more complicated mixed-signal circuits is of crucial importance. The three benchmark circuits are basic, so that it is quite hard to justify the proposed method. Additionally, the cost of the preprocessing should largely increase, and the complexity of task classification should increase as well. The authors should show the feasibility of the proposed method on circuits of large complexity.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on my main concerns listed above, I recommend for reject.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper940 by Reviewer np4B

content.title: Response to Reviewer np4B
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments. Here are the authors’ responses:  

1. (Responses to 1, 4). The comparison is fair and the cost of task pruning is included. First of all, clustering-based task pruning is not data preprocessing. Task pruning is in the loop of RoDesigner. It selects the tasks for the next round of multi-task training based on current solutions and performances. The simulation cost of each pruning is running simulations for all tasks/corners. Such cost has been already included in the comparison. The cost reduction stems from the fewer times we need to interact with the full tasks. RoDesiger trains the agent with the proxy pruned task set and only needs to interact with the full task set when doing task pruning. Baseline line methods have to train on the full task set. Since RoDesigner can achieve all the tasks eventually, the number of queries into the full task set is reduced by a lot compared to baseline methods. 
  

2. (Responses to 2, 4). Multi-task training and task pruning both contribute to cost reduction and they are proposed together as the RoDesigner. Task pruning is not the only key to the improvement. We’ve done an ablation study in Section 4.4. The number of simulation times is reduced from 313200 to 35670 with only multi-task training. The number goes down to 7004 after task pruning. The sampling efficiency improvement from multi-task training roots from leveraging the correlation of tasks and mitigating the competition. Task pruning demonstrates a small subset of full tasks can still be effective. How to do multi-task and choosing which task to train on jointly are both important. RoDesigner studied optimal multi-task setting and task selection and integrated them together to address the variation problem, which is totally different from baseline methods.  

3. (Responses to 5). The complexity of circuits does not solely rely on the number of components. The circuit dynamics, constraints, and variation matter as described in section 4.1. The three benchmarks are representative and important. Large systems are usually built upon them and have similar dynamics. For example, the performance of the complicated mixed-signal system, analog-to-digital converter, is mainly determined by OTA and strongArm latch. Similar benchmarks are also used in many previous works of literature [1],[2].  

     Moreover, task pruning clusters variation corners in the performance domain. It should scale with the size of variation sets rather than circuit complexity. That’s the reason we do scalability in section 4.4. As results indicated, it is scalable to large corner sets.
  
4. This work focuses on addressing the circuit application. We’ve decided to withdraw it.  
   
[1] Wang H, Wang K, Yang J, et al. GCN-RL circuit designer: Transferable transistor sizing with graph neural networks and reinforcement learning[C]//2020 57th ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC). IEEE, 2020: 1-6.  

[2] Settaluri K, Haj-Ali A, Huang Q, et al. AutoCkt: deep reinforcement learning of analog circuit designs[C]//2020 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference & Exhibition (DATE). IEEE, 2020: 490-495.

display_title: Official Review of Paper940 by Reviewer p4Tw

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors proposed a sample-efficient multi-task training method for analog circuit design.
A specific set of the PVT variations of the circuit that determines the performance of the circuit configuration is treated as a different task, and the actor-critic network is trained so that the circuit configuration provided by the actor successfully completes the tasks, i.e. meets the performance target with different variations. 
The sets of variations used for training is sampled using clustering for efficient (in terms of the number of circuit simulations) training.
Using three different benchmarks on circuit sizing, the proposed method significantly reduced the simulation cost for circuit design compared to existing methods.
content.main_review:
This paper is well-written and clearly describes the problem setting and training procedure.
The analog circuit design has been a job of a human expert, and the proposed method using multi-task RL seems like an effective solution.
Task-pruning based on clustering seems also well-suited for the problem setting.

However, this work focuses on the application of the existing learning algorithm, and there seems not much improvement on the learning algorithm itself.
It seems more suitable to be published in design automation conferences/journals.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposed an interesting application of multi-task RL on analog circuit design and showed a clear improvement compared to existing methods.
However, I doubt that the focus of the paper is fit for the ICLR conference.
